Analysis note: onboarding redesign (EXP-912)

We tracked weekly active users (WAU) for six weeks after launch. In the treatment arm, WAU rose from 41.2k to 44.9k, while the control group, which kept the old onboarding flow, stayed near 41k.

The control group is a randomized comparison for this one experiment. The holdout group is different: it is a standing 5% slice of users excluded from every feature launch this quarter, so we can measure cumulative drift across all launches, not just this one.

WAU in the holdout group also drifted up, by about 0.8k, which suggests part of the lift in treatment is seasonal. We therefore report the WAU lift against the control group, and use the holdout group only as a sanity check on the overall trend.

A follow-up on retention by cohort is planned for next sprint.
items.notes: I only added paragraph breaks and used the WAU abbreviation you had already defined. Wording, numbers and the control/holdout distinction are unchanged. Your seasonality reading was kept as written; I did not assess its support, since only the note itself was provided.

items.output: We tested a 14-day trial against the current 7-day trial, with 9,400 trials per arm over eight weeks. The test covered self-serve signups only. Trial-to-paid conversion rose from 11.8% to 14.1%, a lift of 2.3 percentage points. Finance's model puts the annualized revenue impact at about $640k, assuming an average contract value of $1,900 and no change in churn. Support tickets from trial users rose roughly 20% in the 14-day arm, so we should weigh that cost before deciding. The decision meeting is on November 19.
items.notes: One change: your draft said about $940k, but your notes give ~$640k for the Finance model, so I changed it to $640k. If $940k is the newer figure, restore it. The rest already read cleanly and is unchanged.

**Biggest problem:** The piece announces "an exciting new chapter" but never says what changed, so every sentence is placeholder language that could sit in any team's announcement.

## Critical
*Tells that make the whole piece read as machine-written at a glance, or that distort meaning or trust.*

- **Quote:**
  - "drive meaningful impact"
  - "delivering best-in-class solutions that empower stakeholders and unlock new opportunities across the organization"
  - "deliver value at scale"
  - "unlock the full potential of our data"
  **Tell:** H10 — Vague abstraction
  **Why:** ×4 abstractions that name no project, result, or change, so the reader learns nothing about what the team will do.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: the specific projects or results this refers to]"
- **Quote:**
  - "an exciting new chapter for our data science team"
  - "We believe this journey will be transformative for everyone involved."
  **Tell:** S1 — Significance inflation
  **Why:** ×2 claims of importance with no change named to back them; the draft never says what the new chapter is or who is transformed.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: what changes for the data science team]"

## Moderate
*Clear tells a careful reader notices, but that don't dominate the piece.*

- **Quote:**
  - "leverage the power of data"
  - "fast-paced landscape"
  - "best-in-class solutions"
  - "embracing a growth mindset"
  - "embark on this exciting journey"
  **Tell:** L1 — AI vocabulary words (tiered)
  **Why:** ×5 Tier-1 words (leverage, landscape, best-in-class, embrace, embark) spread across all three paragraphs, with a Tier-2 cluster (foster, navigate, empower) on top.
  **Fix:** "use data", "today", "solutions", "working together", "start"
- **Quote:**
  - "Our team is deeply committed to delivering best-in-class solutions that empower stakeholders and unlock new opportunities across the organization."
  - "Going forward, we will continue to foster a culture of collaboration, innovation, and continuous improvement."
  - "By working together and embracing a growth mindset, we will navigate challenges, seize opportunities, and deliver value at scale."
  **Tell:** T10 — Treadmill effect (low information density)
  **Why:** ×3 restatements of the same move ("we are committed to good things"), one per paragraph; any of them could be deleted or swapped with another and nothing would be lost.
  **Fix:** "Our team is committed to delivering solutions for stakeholders."
- **Quote:**
  - "a culture of collaboration, innovation, and continuous improvement"
  - "navigate challenges, seize opportunities, and deliver value at scale"
  **Tell:** T1 — Rule of three
  **Why:** ×2 triads in consecutive sentences, the second padded to reach three.
  **Fix:** "a culture of collaboration"
- **Quote:**
  - "Together, we can achieve great things."
  - "We are grateful for your ongoing support and look forward to partnering with you as we embark on this exciting journey."
  - "Stay tuned for more updates as we continue to unlock the full potential of our data."
  **Tell:** H3 — Generic positive conclusions
  **Why:** ×3 upbeat closers in the last paragraph, none of which carries a fact, a decision, or a next action.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: the next concrete update and when it will arrive]"
- **Quote:** "In today's fast-paced landscape, it is more important than ever"
  **Tell:** H1 — Filler phrases
  **Why:** runway before the point; the sentence works without it.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: what the team will do with data]"

## Minor
*Cosmetic or low-frequency tells only a scan catches.*

- **Quote:**
  - "We are thrilled to announce"
  - "this exciting journey"
  **Tell:** S6 — Promotional / advertisement language
  **Why:** ×2 self-congratulating adjectives (thrilled, exciting) that tell the reader how to feel instead of what happened.
  **Fix:** "We are announcing", "this work"

## What already reads well
- Nothing here reads well yet: every sentence carries a flagged pattern.

Hi team,

Here are the backtest results for our fraud detection model on Tallow Bank's card business. In backtesting on March through August data, the model caught approximately 38% more fraudulent transactions than the current rules engine at the same false-positive rate (95% CI: 31% to 45%). This result applies only to card-not-present transactions, which make up roughly 60% of volume; in-store transactions were not part of the backtest.

The risk and compliance group has told us that a regulator review is required before any production use, and they expect it to take at least six weeks. Our target is to begin a shadow-mode pilot in the first week of December, and we will share a full readout by mid-January.

Update on the push-notification permission prompt test for the Lumen Budgeting app: the new pre-permission screen increased opt-in rate by 7 percentage points (from 44% to 51%; 95% CI 4 to 10 points) among new iOS users.

This suggests that explaining the value before the system dialog may help users feel more comfortable saying yes, though we did not test the mechanism directly.

Android users were excluded from the test because the permission model differs, so we cannot say whether the result generalizes. We also saw no change in 30-day retention among those who opted in, but the sample was small, so this is inconclusive rather than reassuring.

Weekly orders fell 9% week over week, from 15,600 to 14,200, for the week of October 12.

The decline began on October 14, the same day the v3.8 checkout release went live. Mobile web orders dropped 13%, compared with 4% on desktop, which is consistent with the release adding friction on mobile web. SRE reports no spike in checkout error logs.

We have not ruled out the paid search budget cut on October 13; Marketing has not yet sent the channel breakdown. We are going to roll back v3.8. If the release is the main cause, we expect orders to recover by next week.
items.notes:
Your notes don't support several claims in the draft, so I restated them at the strength the notes allow:
- "The decline was caused by the v3.8 checkout release" became timing (the drop began the same day v3.8 went live). Mobile web falling more than desktop is described as "consistent with" added friction. The notes don't establish that friction.
- "The problem is purely one of user experience" is cut. The notes say only that SRE saw no error spike.
- "Marketing's paid search budget change is not a factor" became "we have not ruled out" the Oct 13 cut, since the channel breakdown is still outstanding.
- "Expect orders to recover by next week" is now conditional on the release being the main cause.
The rollback decision is kept as you wrote it. If you have evidence that settles the cause, restore the stronger wording.

# Store Labor Scheduling Pilot: Findings

## Summary

Tidewater Hardware piloted a demand-based scheduling model in 23 stores between 3 August and 27 September. Understaffed hours fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours in pilot stores, while labor spend stayed within 1% of plan. Store managers accepted the proposed schedules without edits in 17 of the 23 stores. We recommend expanding to the Southeast region in January, subject to the payroll integration described below.

## What we did

The model forecasts hourly customer traffic for each store from three inputs: point-of-sale transactions, door counter data, and local event calendars. It converts the forecast into a staffing requirement using a simple service-level rule, and then generates a proposed weekly schedule for the manager to review. Managers could accept the schedule as is or edit it. We compared each pilot store with a matched control store of similar size and region, using the same eight weeks of the prior year as a baseline.

## Results

Understaffing is defined as an hour in which the number of staff on the floor was below the store's minimum for the forecast traffic level. Across the 23 pilot stores it fell from 14.2% to 9.8% of open hours. In the matched control stores it moved from 14.0% to 13.1%, so the net improvement attributable to the model is about 3.5 percentage points.

Labor spend in pilot stores was 0.6% above plan, compared with 0.9% above plan in control stores. We do not read much into the difference.

Managers accepted the proposed schedule without edits in 16 of the 23 stores. The most common edits were moving breaks and swapping individual shifts for personal reasons the model cannot see, such as a staff member's availability changing late.

## Limitations

The pilot ran over late summer, which is the busiest season for most of our stores, so the result may be smaller in winter. Two stores in the pilot had a manager change in the middle of the period. Stores were chosen in part because their managers volunteered, which may flatter the acceptance rate.

## Next steps

Payroll integration is the main blocker. Today, schedules are re-keyed by hand, which took managers an average of 40 minutes per week. Platform engineering has committed to delivering the integration by 30 November. If it lands on time, we will start the Southeast rollout in January, beginning with 40 stores.
items.notes: The document was already well organized, so I made only two small edits: a comma after "Today" in Next steps, and "committed to deliver" became "committed to delivering". One conflict needs your call. The Summary says managers accepted schedules without edits in 17 of the 23 stores, but the Results section says 16 of the 23. I didn't pick one. Also, the Summary gives the raw drop from 14.2% to 9.8%, while Results shows the control-adjusted figure of about 3.5 percentage points. You may want leadership to see the adjusted figure first.

**Biggest problem:** The "It's not X, it's Y" construction recurs five times, so the draft reads as one repeated rhetorical move rather than a series of facts.

## Critical
*Tells that make the whole piece read as machine-written at a glance, or that distort meaning or trust.*

- **Quote:**
  - "It's not a reporting tool, it's a decision engine."
  - "It's not about running more tests, it's about asking sharper questions."
  - "It's not a gate for launches, it's a conversation starter."
  - "It's not a finished product, it's a living system that improves with each experiment."
  - "It's not just infrastructure, it's the way we learn."
  **Tell:** T2 — Negative parallelism / tailing negation
  **Why:** ×5 across three of the four paragraphs, two of them closing a paragraph; the catalog's own guidance is one per piece at most.
  **Fix:** "It's a decision engine." "It's about asking sharper questions." "It's a conversation starter." "It improves with each experiment." "It's the way we learn."

## Moderate
*Clear tells a careful reader notices, but that don't dominate the piece.*

- **Quote:**
  - "The cultural shift matters as much as the tooling."
  - "It's not just infrastructure, it's the way we learn."
  **Tell:** N1 — Over-explained theme (states its own moral)
  **Why:** ×2 sentences that name the lesson instead of letting the facts carry it (advisory, document-level); the closing line is the draft's final word although a concrete plan sits just before it.
  **Fix:** end on "We plan to extend it to the pricing and notifications groups next quarter."
- **Quote:** "Product managers tell us they now read experiment results before they read opinions."
  **Tell:** S4 — Vague attribution / weasel words
  **Why:** attributes a claim to a group with no count or named source, so a reader cannot check it.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: how many product managers said this, or a named source]"
- **Quote:** "Looking ahead, the platform will keep growing with the teams that use it."
  **Tell:** H4 — Generic future-narrative closers
  **Why:** a prediction with no testable content; the next sentence has the real plan.
  **Fix:** delete it and keep "We plan to extend it to the pricing and notifications groups next quarter."

## Minor
*Cosmetic or low-frequency tells only a scan catches.*

- **Quote:** "a living system that improves with each experiment"
  **Tell:** L7 — Mannered prose (metaphor where a literal phrase exists)
  **Why:** advisory; a bespoke metaphor where a plain phrase is available.
  **Fix:** "It improves with each experiment."
- **Quote:** "asking sharper questions"
  **Tell:** H10 — Vague abstraction
  **Why:** names no example of a sharper question, so the claim cannot be pictured.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: one example of a sharper question analysts now ask]"

## What already reads well
- "You might think that a stricter review step would slow teams down, but the data shows median time from proposal to launch fell from 19 days to 12 days since we introduced it." It raises a plausible objection and answers it with a measured before-and-after number, so I set this "you might think" setup aside instead of flagging it.
- "The platform team holds weekly office hours where anyone can bring a half-formed idea and leave with a testable design." It names a concrete mechanism and its outcome.

Hi Priya, welcome to the team!

A few things that helped me when I started. The churn dashboard refreshes at 6 a.m. Pacific, so if the numbers look odd before then, they're yesterday's. Our definition of an active user is anyone with at least one session in the last 28 days; I know that's different from what Growth uses, and it trips everyone up at first.

Please ask questions early and often. Nobody here will think less of you for it, and honestly, the best fixes to our docs have come from newcomers asking what something means. I'm free Thursday afternoon if you'd like to walk through the pipeline together.

# Search Ranking Test Readout: Pinewood Books

## Summary

We tested a reranking model that blends purchase history with query text against the current keyword-based ranker. Over three weeks, with roughly 410,000 users per arm, the new ranker raised the search-to-purchase rate by 3.1% relative (from 5.80% to 5.98%) with no meaningful change in page load time. We recommend shipping it to all web users in the week of 7 December.

## Background

Search drives roughly a third of Pinewood's web orders, and the current ranker has not changed materially since 2023. Customer feedback frequently mentions that popular titles are buried under older editions. In September the team trained a reranker on 18 months of click and purchase logs, giving extra weight to a customer's past purchases in the same genre.

## Method

Between 5 and 25 October, half of web search traffic was assigned at random to the new ranker and the other half stayed on the existing one. Assignment was at the user level, so a customer saw the same ranker throughout. Each arm included about 401,000 users. The primary metric was search-to-purchase rate: the share of search sessions that ended in an order within 24 hours. Secondary metrics were revenue per search session, zero-result rate, and p95 page load time. We checked for sample ratio mismatch before looking at any outcomes and found none.

## Results

Search-to-purchase rate was 5.80% in control and 5.98% in treatment, an absolute difference of 0.18 percentage points and a relative lift of 3.1%. The 95% confidence interval for the absolute difference is 0.09 to 0.27 points. Revenue per search session rose by 1.9%, though the interval for that metric includes zero. The zero-result rate was unchanged at 2.4%. The p95 page load time increased from 1.42 to 1.44 seconds, which we do not consider material.

## Caveats

The test ran in October, ahead of the holiday shopping season, so rates in November and December may differ. Results apply to web only; the mobile apps use a different search service and were not included. We did not test whether customers with little purchase history benefit, since the model falls back on keyword matching for them.

## Next steps

Engineering will complete the load test by 20 November. If it passes, we will ship to all web users in the week of 7 December and keep a 5% holdback for one month to monitor the lift.
items.notes: Light touch: I changed nothing, since I found no errors. One conflict is yours to resolve. The Summary says roughly 410,000 users per arm, but Method says about 401,000 per arm. I didn't pick one. Everything else (the 5.80% to 5.98%, the 3.1% relative lift, the 0.18-point difference and its interval) agrees across sections.

Subject: Update on the Churn Early-Warning Model

Hi Dana,

I wanted to share some encouraging news about the churn early-warning model. On the holdout set of about 62,000 accounts, it achieved a precision of 0.71 (95% CI 0.68 to 0.74) among the top-decile flagged accounts. This holds only for postpaid customers; prepaid accounts were not evaluated because the data was not sufficiently available.

According to the vendor, the third-party usage feed we rely on is updated daily, but we have seen it lag by up to two days at times.

The model could let our retention team take proactive action. Let me know if you have any questions or would like to discuss.

Best,
Ravi

Pricing test result: the $9 tier lost. Conversion fell from 4.1% to 3.6% over 21 days, with about 58,000 visitors per arm. Revenue per visitor was flat, within noise. Mobile and desktop moved together, so no segment story. I'd stop the test and keep $7. Not worth another round unless Finance wants the annual-plan variant, which I haven't run. Notebook is in the team repo if anyone wants to check my work.
items.notes: No changes. It's already short, leads with the result, and states the recommendation and what you didn't test.

**Biggest problem:** Apart from one measured result, the draft tells readers a "next phase" is starting without saying what changes, so it reads as interchangeable corporate boilerplate wrapped around a single real fact.

## Critical
*Tells that make the whole piece read as machine-written at a glance, or that distort meaning or trust.*

- **Quote:**
  - "represents a significant step forward in how we approach data infrastructure"
  - "By aligning around a common vision, we are positioning ourselves for long-term success."
  **Tell:** S1 — Significance inflation
  **Why:** ×2 claims of importance or success that name no concrete change; the only evidence in the piece (the latency result) is never connected to either claim.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: what changes in the platform modernization effort, beyond the Atlas latency result]"
- **Quote:**
  - "streamline workflows and enhance the overall user experience"
  - "designed to meet the evolving needs of the business"
  - "help us shape what comes next"
  **Tell:** H10 — Vague abstraction
  **Why:** ×3 abstractions where a fact belongs; the reader cannot tell which workflows change or what users will notice.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: which workflows change and what users will notice]"

## Moderate
*Clear tells a careful reader notices, but that don't dominate the piece.*

- **Quote:**
  - "leverage cross-functional synergies"
  - "holistic"
  - "streamline workflows"
  - "data ecosystem"
  **Tell:** L1 — AI vocabulary words (tiered)
  **Why:** ×4 words (leverage and synergies, holistic, streamline, ecosystem) concentrated in the last two paragraphs; two Tier-1 words plus Tier-2 words in one stretch makes a cluster.
  **Fix:** "use cross-functional work to simplify workflows", "complete", "data infrastructure"
- **Quote:**
  - "holistic, scalable, and designed to meet the evolving needs of the business"
  - "stay engaged, share feedback, and help us shape what comes next"
  **Tell:** T1 — Rule of three
  **Why:** ×2 triads, each with a third item that is a longer clause added to reach three.
  **Fix:** "share feedback"
- **Quote:** "it reflects our shared commitment to excellence"
  **Tell:** S2 — Symbolic gloss / meaning-telling
  **Why:** attaches a meaning to the initiative with no fact that warrants it.
  **Fix:** delete ", and it reflects our shared commitment to excellence"
- **Quote:** "We are excited to share the next phase of our platform modernization effort."
  **Tell:** H7 — Signposting / announcements
  **Why:** announces that something will be shared; the following sentences never say what the next phase is.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: what the next phase is]"
- **Quote:**
  - "Thank you for being part of this journey."
  - "Together, we will build a stronger, more resilient data ecosystem for the future."
  **Tell:** H3 — Generic positive conclusions
  **Why:** ×2 upbeat closers that carry no fact, decision, or next action, while a concrete sentence is available earlier in the draft.
  **Fix:** end on "Last week's load test of the Atlas feature store showed median read latency dropping from 840 ms to 210 ms."

## Minor
*Cosmetic or low-frequency tells only a scan catches.*

- **Quote:** "We encourage everyone to stay engaged, share feedback, and help us shape what comes next."
  **Tell:** C1 — Chatbot artifacts
  **Why:** a generic invitation that names no channel, owner, or date for the feedback.
  **Fix:** "[NEEDS: where and by when to send feedback]"

## What already reads well
- "Last week's load test of the Atlas feature store showed median read latency dropping from 840 ms to 210 ms." It names the system, the test, the metric, and before and after values a reader can check.
